extracted.intended_audience: U.S. individual taxpayers who need more time to file their federal income tax return (general public)
extracted.subtask_description: Step-by-step guidance on when and how U.S. individual taxpayers can request an automatic extension to file their federal tax return (Form 4868 or electronic payment) and the consequences of not filing/paying on time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension to file is not an extension to pay taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The IRS reminds taxpayers 'an extension to file is not an extension to pay taxes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you owe taxes, you must send a payment to cover it or face penalties on the amount owed. Only the filing deadline gets an extension; taxes are still owed by April 15.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information required on the extension application
rubrics_metrics.description: The extension form requires basic identification and an estimate of tax liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You'll basically need your name, address, Social Security number, and estimated taxes owed or refunded to request an automatic extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to file an extension
rubrics_metrics.description: File an extension if you are missing information you can't obtain quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common missing items include K-1s from third parties. Filing an extension gives you more time to gather required information.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to request an extension if you have no taxes due
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals, regardless of income, can request an automatic six-month filing extension using IRS Free File or Form 4868.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use IRS.gov/freefile to request the automatic six-month extension, or file Form 4868 (must be mailed before April 15 if you mail it).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to request an extension if you owe money
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting an electronic payment and selecting Form 4868/extension as the payment type counts as an extension without needing Form 4868.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxpayers can make an electronic payment and choose the extension option; the IRS will automatically record the extension, eliminating the need to file a separate Form 4868.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mailing/postmark timing and postal-delay precautions
rubrics_metrics.description: If mailing Form 4868, it must be sent before April 15 and be postmarked on time to be valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postal delays can cause a timely-mailed form to be treated as late. If short on time, get a hand-stamped postmark at the local post office or consider filing online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special additional time for certain taxpayers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some groups (disaster victims, those living abroad, military members in combat zones) may have extra time to file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check IRS rules for exceptions that grant extended filing deadlines to these populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to file penalty (late filing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The IRS charges a failure to file penalty if you don't file on time: 5% of the tax owed each month (or part of a month) up to a maximum of 25%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the return is more than 60 days late there's also a minimum penalty: the lesser of $525 this year or 100% of the tax owed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to pay penalty (late payment)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you fail to pay the full amount owed, the IRS charges 0.5% for each month (or part of a month) up to 25% of the unpaid tax, starting from the due date until paid in full.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The penalty increases to 1% per month if the tax remains unpaid 10 days after the IRS issues a notice of intent to seize assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest on unpaid taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The IRS charges interest on any balance due, compounded daily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The interest rate is determined quarterly as the federal short-term rate plus 3%. (Example: in the first three months of the year the rate was 7%.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No penalty if you owe nothing or are due a refund (but file ASAP)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no penalty for filing late if you don't owe money or are owed a refund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, the IRS encourages filing as soon as possible because you cannot receive your refund until you file the return.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to estimate tax liability for payment with extension
rubrics_metrics.description: "Multiply the additional income by your marginal tax rate to start," then add cushion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When estimating taxes owed to send with an extension, use your marginal tax rate on additional income and consider adding extra margin to cover unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you can't pay in full, apply for a payment plan
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can't afford to pay your tax bill in full by April 15, you should apply for a payment plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once you apply, the IRS will notify you almost immediately if you're approved. The IRS publishes the different payment plan options you can choose from.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check state tax deadlines and extension requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a federal extension does not automatically cover state tax obligations in all states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some states have their own extension forms and requirements; some provide an automatic extension or rely on the federal extension. Know your state's rules to determine if you need to file a separate state extension.
